## Summary

**Background.** Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) is used for
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis after allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), but its impact on
infection risk versus longer-established prophylaxis regimens has not
been systematically quantified.

**Methods.** In this systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis, we
searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS from database inception to April 30,
2026 for studies comparing PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis with alternative
regimens in adult allo-HSCT recipients. Comparisons were PTCy versus
calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) plus methotrexate or mycophenolate (C1),
PTCy versus anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG; C2), and within-PTCy variants
(C3). Outcomes were overall survival (OS; primary), non-relapse
mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV, CMV reactivation, bloodstream
infection (BSI), and invasive fungal infection (IFI). We fitted Bayesian
random-effects binomial-logistic models to estimate infection risks.
PROSPERO registration: CRD420261372156.

**Findings.** Of 4145 records, 250 studies (523 arms; 177 849 patients)
were included, 105 in the meta-analysis. In C1 (72 studies), PTCy was
associated with better OS (odds ratio 0·73 \[95% credible interval
0·58–0·89\]) and less acute GVHD (0·58 \[0·44–0·76\]); CMV and BSI
estimates were elevated but imprecise (1·20 \[0·87–1·65\]; 2·17
\[0·86–4·39\], the latter from four culture-confirmed studies). In C2
(27 studies), OS favoured PTCy versus ATG (0·75 \[0·43–1·28\]) and CMV
did not differ (0·86 \[0·51–1·42\]). The increased CMV estimate was
larger in studies published from 2020 onward (1·43 \[0·97–2·06\]) .GRADE
certainty was very low for all pre-specified outcomes.

**Interpretation.** PTCy is associated with better survival and less
GVHD versus CNI-based prophylaxis, with uncertain benefit versus ATG.
Infection estimates were compatible with increased CMV and bacterial
infection risk versus less T-cell-depleting regimens, but estimates were
less precise. CMV direction fits a T-cell-depletion class effect; BK
virus elevation was similar across comparators, compatible with a
cyclophosphamide-specific effect.

**Funding.** There was no funding source for this study.

## Research in context

::: panel
### Evidence before this study

We searched PubMed, EMBASE and SCOPUS for systematic reviews and
meta-analyses of post-transplant cyclophosphamide in allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation published from database
inception to April 30, 2026, using the terms "post-transplant
cyclophosphamide" AND ("meta-analysis" OR "systematic review"). We
identified ten comparative meta-analyses [@yu2019; @poonsombudlert2019;
@gagelmann2019; @arcuri2019; @gao2021; @arcuri2021; @tang2023; @luo2025;
@jin2025; @shahsavand2026] encompassing 6–30 studies each. All evaluated
survival and GVHD outcomes; only three [@tang2023; @luo2025; @jin2025]
pooled infection outcomes between prophylaxis regimens, each with few
contributing studies per infection type and comparison. No prior study
compared PTCy against both CNI-based and ATG-based comparators in a
unified framework, and none has proposed a mechanistic explanation for
the apparently contradictory infection findings across comparator
contexts.

### Added value of this study

In this large systematic review and meta-analysis (250 studies, 177 849
patients), we were able to systematically pool CMV, bloodstream
infection, and invasive fungal infection risk in the context of GVHD and
survival within the same analytic framework. Its dual-comparator design
suggests that the estimated effect of PTCy on CMV risk may reverse
direction depending on the comparator's own T-cell depletion depth,
although the contrast is indirect and not formally resolved. Elevated
average infection risk was estimated versus CNI-based (odds ratio 1·20
\[0·87–1·65\]) but not ATG-based (0·86 \[0·51–1·42\]) prophylaxis, a
directional pattern compatible with expected degree of T-cell depletion.
However, a formal meta-regression on comparator class did not resolve
the difference (ratio of odds ratios 0·71 \[0·41–1·20\]; appendix S9).

### Implications of all the available evidence

PTCy is associated with better overall survival and less GVHD across
comparator types, although certainty of evidence is very low for all
pre-specified outcomes. Infection estimates are imprecise and pattern
differently by pathogen: CMV estimates are directionally consistent with
the comparator's T-cell depletion depth, whereas BK virus elevation was
similar across comparators, compatible with a cyclophosphamide-specific
effect. These results suggest that clinical strategies to mitigate these
risks should target T-cell reconstitution (adoptive T-cell therapy,
optimised letermovir prophylaxis, earlier immunosuppression tapering)
rather than PTCy avoidance. Within-PTCy regimen variants show no
detectable differences, but with k = 4–7 per outcome this is absence of
evidence, not evidence of equivalence.
:::

## Introduction

Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) has transformed allogeneic
haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) by enabling
transplantation across HLA barriers and simplifying graft-versus-host
disease (GVHD) prophylaxis.[@odonnell2002] Originally developed for
haploidentical transplants[@luznik2008], PTCy is now widely used across
all donor types[@kanakry2016], and as shown in the BMT CTN 1703/1801
randomised controlled trial (RCT), is superior to conventional
calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-based prophylaxis in terms of GVHD-free,
relapse-free survival.[@bolanosmeade2023]

Uncertainty remains regarding a possible increased risk of infection
with PTCy versus more estalbished prophylaxis regimens after transplant.
Compared to CNI-based prophylaxis, CIBMTR registry studies have reported
that PTCy-based regimens are associated with increased cytomegalovirus
(CMV) reactivation[@goldsmith2021] and a higher incidence of bacterial
bloodstream infections with comparable or reduced rates of fungal
infections.[@papanicolaou2024] This excess risk, however, has been
difficult to quantify because prior meta-analyses have been restricted
to single comparisons, limited to 6–20 studies, and have rarely included
infection as a primary outcome. The absence of a unified analytic
framework spanning multiple comparator contexts raises a fundamental
question: are infection risks attributable to PTCy itself, or to the
depth of T-cell depletion inherent to any intensive GVHD prophylaxis?
Answering this question requires simultaneous comparison of PTCy against
both less depleting (CNI plus methotrexate) and more depleting
(anti-thymocyte globulin \[ATG\]) regimens.

To address this question, we conducted a systematic review and Bayesian
meta-analysis to simultaneously evaluate survival, GVHD, and infection
outcomes of PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis across three pre-specified
comparisons.

## Methods

### Search strategy and selection criteria

This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance
with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with PROSPERO
(CRD420261372156). We searched EMBASE, PubMed, and SCOPUS from database
inception to April 30, 2026 for studies comparing PTCy-based GVHD
prophylaxis with alternative regimens in adult (≥18 years) allo-HSCT
recipients published in English. The complete search strategy for PubMed
is provided in the [appendix (pp
2–4)](appendix-preview.html#s1.-search-strategy). Reference lists of
included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched. No language
restrictions were applied at the search stage; studies not available in
English were excluded at full-text review.

Studies were eligible if they reported at least one pre-specified
outcome with extractable event counts (numerator and denominator) for at
least two arms differing in GVHD prophylaxis strategy. Conference
abstracts were excluded. We defined three pre-specified comparisons: C1,
PTCy (with or without CNI or mycophenolate mofetil \[MMF\]) versus CNI
plus methotrexate (MTX) or MMF without ATG or T-cell depletion; C2, PTCy
versus ATG-based prophylaxis; and C3, within-PTCy regimen variants.

Two reviewers (MS and REL) screened titles and abstracts using the
Covidence platform (www.coevidence.org) and extracted data from PDFs
files into a structured template ([appendix p
5](appendix-preview.html#s3.-characteristics-of-included-studies)) using
AI tools (Claude Code, Anthropic, Inc.). All extracted values were
manually verified by two investigators against source publications. Risk
of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I for observational studies and RoB 2
for RCTs. Studies sharing patient cohorts were flagged and the most
comprehensive publication was designated as primary publication for each
cohort–outcome combination. All pooled estimates reported here were
derived from this cohort-deduplicated dataset, so that no patient
contributes more than once to any single outcome. The cohort overlap map
is provided in the [appendix (p
24)](appendix-preview.html#s12.-cohort-overlap).

### Outcomes

The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), analysed as all-cause
mortality (death as the event) at the reported timepoint. Secondary
outcomes included non-relapse mortality (NRM), acute GVHD grade II–IV
(at day +100), chronic GVHD (moderate to severe), CMV reactivation
(any), bloodstream infection (BSI, any pathogen), invasive fungal
infection (IFI, any), relapse-related mortality (RRM), BK virus
reactivation, and infection-related mortality (IRM).

### Statistical analysis

We fitted Bayesian random-effects binomial-logistic regression models
using `brms` (version 2.23.0) with an `rstan` backend in R (version
4.6.0). The primary model (M1) estimated the PTCy treatment effect with
a random intercept and a random PTCy-effect slope for study, so that
pooled effects average over between-study heterogeneity in the treatment
effect. Each study contributed a single row per outcome with a preferred
timepoint where reported (day +100 or +180 for early outcomes, one year
for late outcomes), otherwise the nearest reported (fallback) timepoint
was used so no within-study correlation across timepoints arises. An
indicator variable distinguished fallback from preferred timepoints.
Weakly informative priors were specified: N(0, 2·5) on fixed effects,
N(0, 1·5) on the intercept, and Student t(3, 0, 1) on the between-study
standard deviations (τ). Four chains of 4000 iterations (1000 warmup)
were run with `adapt_delta` = 0·95 (increased to 0·99 where divergent
transitions occurred). Convergence was assessed by R̂ and effective
sample size. Single-arm descriptive studies (n = 26) were retained for
the PRISMA flow diagram and descriptive tabulation only; because they
report no comparator arm, they contribute no outcome data to any
comparative model, all of which are restricted to studies reporting
event counts for both a PTCy and a non-PTCy arm. Arms receiving PTCy
together with anti-thymocyte globulin were classified as PTCy arms in
all three comparisons; a sensitivity analysis excluding the C2 studies
containing such arms is reported in appendix S9.

An exploratory steroid-adjustment model (M2), a post-hoc amendment to
the registered protocol (appendix S13), added arm-level systemic
corticosteroid exposure as a covariate. Because the covariate is
post-treatment and arm-level, and in most arms approximated from acute
GVHD incidence rather than directly reported, M2 estimates no indirect
effect and is reported only in the appendix (S9), together with its
definition, provenance, results, and a matched-set comparison against
M1.

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses included restriction to publications
from 2020 onward (a publication-year, not enrollment-era, subset,
spanning the letermovir-introduction period), to haploidentical-dominant
cohorts (≥50% haploidentical donors), and leave-one-out analysis. Hazard
ratios were not pooled in the primary analysis because most studies
reported only event counts or Kaplan–Meier estimates at fixed
timepoints; in a post-hoc sensitivity analysis, the reported
overall-survival hazard ratios (multivariable-adjusted where available,
one per study, direction harmonised to PTCy versus comparator with death
as the event) were pooled two-stage under a random-effects model
(appendix S9). Frequentist random-effects models (restricted maximum
likelihood \[REML\], `metafor` version 5.0.1) were fitted as concordance
checks. Publication bias was assessed using robust Bayesian
model-averaging (RoBMA). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the
GRADE framework adapted for observational evidence.

### Role of the funding source

There was no funding source for this study.

## Results

### Search results and study characteristics

The database search identified 4145 records (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061,
SCOPUS 481), of which 1220 were duplicates (@fig-prisma). After
screening 2925 titles and abstracts, 517 articles were sought for
full-text review; 52 could not be retrieved or were not in English. Of
465 full-text articles assessed, 215 were excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n214)),
leaving 250 studies for the systematic review. Of these, 105 unique
studies contained sufficient outcome data to contribute to the
meta-analysis across three comparisons: C1 (72 studies), C2 (27
studies), and C3 (13 studies). Seven studies contributed to more than
one comparison, so the comparison counts sum to 112 rather than 105; the
per-outcome attrition from extraction to pooling is given in appendix
S12.

The 224 comparative studies encompassed 518 arms and 177 461 patients
(@tbl-characteristics). Most were retrospective cohorts (131 \[58%\]) or
registry analyses (62 \[28%\]); 14 (6%) were RCTs. Median publication
year was 2023 (IQR 2021–24), with median follow-up of 26 months (IQR
20–36). PTCy arms were predominantly haploidentical donor transplants
(127 \[47%\]) whereas comparator arms were predominantly matched
unrelated (94 \[38%\]) or matched sibling (54 \[22%\]) donor
transplants.

### Risk of bias

Of 220 comparative observational studies assessed with ROBINS-I, 149
(68%) were at serious risk of bias and 71 (32%) at moderate risk,
primarily due to confounding by donor type and conditioning intensity;
no study was rated low or critical risk ([appendix pp
15–17](appendix-preview.html#s5.-risk-of-bias)). Single-arm descriptive
studies (n = 26) were excluded from the comparative analyses and are not
included in these counts. Of 14 RCTs assessed with RoB 2, 11 had some
concerns, two were at high risk, and one was at low risk of bias.
Because the measurement-of-outcome domain matters most for subjective
endpoints, judgements were reviewed by outcome objectivity: concerns in
the open-label trials centred on clinician-assessed outcomes (GVHD
grading and infection ascertainment; measurement-domain some concerns in
3 of 14 trials), whereas objective outcomes (overall and relapse-related
mortality, laboratory-confirmed bloodstream infection) were at low
measurement-domain risk in every trial.

### Comparison 1: PTCy versus CNI plus MTX or MMF

PTCy was associated with improved OS (k = 29, odds ratio 0·73 [95%
credible interval 0·58–0·89]; @fig-os). NRM showed a non-significant
trend toward benefit (k = 11, 0·84 [0·48–1·28]). Relapse-related
mortality was lower (k = 34, 0·87 \[0·76–0·99\]).

Acute GVHD grade II–IV was substantially less frequent (k = 28, 0·58
\[0·44–0·77\]), as was moderate-to-severe chronic GVHD (k = 18, 0·41
\[0·23–0·72\]).

CMV reactivation was higher on average in the PTCy group, but the
credible interval included the null (k = 21, 1·20 [0·87–1·65];
@fig-cmv). The estimate was larger in studies published from 2020 onward
(k = 16, 1·43 [0·97–2·06]) and in haploidentical-dominant cohorts (k =
12, 1·34 [0·89–1·96]). BSIs likewise favoured the comparator vs. PTCy in
the primary analysis restricted to culture-confirmed day-100 bloodstream
infection (k = 4, 2·17 [0·86–4·39]); no comparison-2 BSI model was
possible. BK virus reactivation showed the largest infection effect with
PTCy, and the only one whose interval excluded the null (k = 11, 2·39
[1·41–3·73]; @fig-infections). The IFI estimate was highly uncertain in
either direction (k = 6, 0·63 [0·19–2·44]), with extreme between-study
heterogeneity in the treatment effect (τ = 1·28). Infection-related
mortality showed no excess with PTCy versus CNI plus MTX or MMF (k = 13,
1·02 \[0·67–1·50\]).

### Comparison 2: PTCy versus ATG

The OS estimate favoured PTCy versus ATG but with substantial
uncertainty (k = 6, odds ratio 0·75 \[0·43–1·28\]). Acute GVHD was less
frequent on average, with the interval just reaching the null (k = 7,
0·53 \[0·23–1·17\]). NRM could not be assessed (k = 2). Relapse-related
mortality was lower, with the interval reaching the null (k = 10, 0·79
\[0·55–1·03\]). CMV reactivation did not differ between strategies (k =
12, 0·86 \[0·51–1·42\]), in contrast with the elevated C1 estimate.
Infection-related mortality did not differ (k = 7, 0·98 \[0·62–1·77\]).
BK virus reactivation was elevated versus ATG (k = 3, 2·49
\[1·09–6·03\]), the only infection estimate in C2 whose interval
excluded the null.

### Comparison 3: within-PTCy variants

No significant differences were detected between PTCy-based regimen
variants for any outcome (OS 0·92, NRM 0·51, acute GVHD 0·43, chronic
GVHD 0·53, relapse-related mortality 0·78; all credible intervals
crossed the null; k = 4–7 per outcome).

### Confounding and robustness analyses

Sensitivity analyses are reported in full in appendix S9. Within-study
donor-type imbalance was small (median between-arm difference in
haploidentical-donor percentage 0), a meta-regression on that difference
was null for every C1 outcome, and in donor-matched subsets (difference
≤15 percentage points) the C1 overall-survival estimate was, if
anything, stronger (0·58 \[0·41–0·78\], k = 21). Trial-only models were
not estimable once cumulative-incidence-derived event counts were
excluded (no more than two trials per outcome retain observed counts),
so the earlier trial-only estimates, which included such counts, are
superseded (appendix S9); observational-only estimates were compatible
with the pooled results (overall survival 0·79 \[0·63–0·96\], k = 26;
acute GVHD 0·60 \[0·44–0·78\], k = 27; chronic GVHD 0·48 \[0·27–0·86\],
k = 14; NRM 0·91 \[0·57–1·36\], k = 10; CMV 1·01 \[0·64–1·64\], k = 7).
Splitting C1 comparators by backbone suggested the survival benefit may
be concentrated against CNI plus MTX (0·56 \[0·34–0·84\], k = 12) rather
than CNI plus MMF (1·10 \[0·45–3·01\], k = 5), although a formal
interaction test did not resolve the difference (ratio of odds ratios
1·82 \[0·76–4·53\]). Restricting CMV to clinically significant infection
rather than any reactivation gave an imprecise estimate compatible with
both a decrease and an increase (0·94 \[0·49–1·71\], k = 8), so that
result is uncertain rather than evidence of no increase. Adjustment for
a letermovir enrolment-era proxy did not change the CMV estimate (1·20
\[0·86–1·67\]); no arm in the publication-2020-onward subset had
recorded letermovir use, and most enrolled before or across the
letermovir era, so the larger estimate in recent publications cannot be
attributed to letermovir adoption.

### Certainty of evidence

GRADE certainty was very low for all pre-specified outcomes
(@tbl-results), reassessed against the post-adjudication random-effects
estimates with publication-bias analyses re-run on the same datasets
([appendix
S10–S11](appendix-preview.html#s11.-grade-certainty-of-evidence-profiles)).
Imprecision was assessed against clinically meaningful thresholds (odds
ratio 0·80 for benefit, 1·25 for harm); downgrades were applied to every
outcome whose credible interval spans the relevant threshold or the null
— all pre-specified outcomes except C1 acute GVHD, whose interval lies
entirely below 0·80. Secondary outcomes added by protocol amendment were
rated under the same framework (appendix S11): certainty was low for BK
virus reactivation versus CNI-based prophylaxis (2·39 \[1·41–3·73\];
interval entirely above 1·25) and very low for C1 relapse-related
mortality (0·87 \[0·76–0·99\]; interval spans the 0·80 benefit
threshold), C1 and C2 infection-related mortality, C2 relapse-related
mortality, and C2 BK virus reactivation (k = 3). C1 OS and C1 acute GVHD
were additionally downgraded for publication bias: robust Bayesian
model-averaging found strong evidence of bias for both (BF~bias~ 10·4
and 10·9), and the bias-adjusted estimates are essentially null (OS 0·97
\[0·71–1·16\]; acute GVHD 0·96 \[0·57–1·38\]; appendix S10), so the
unadjusted survival and acute GVHD benefits are not robust to
publication-bias adjustment.

## Discussion

This review of 250 studies (523 arms; over 177 000 patients) provides a
unified Bayesian evaluation of survival, GVHD, and infection outcomes
with PTCy-based prophylaxis, supporting mechanistic interpretation not
possible in single-comparison reviews.

PTCy was associated with less acute GVHD grade II–IV versus CNI plus MTX
or MMF (odds ratio 0·58; from a median comparator-arm incidence of 33%,
about 108 fewer cases per 1000 patients) and versus ATG (0·51, with the
interval just reaching the null), with correspondingly lower chronic
GVHD. Overall survival was better for PTCy versus CNI-based prophylaxis
(0·73 \[0·58–0·89\]); against a median comparator-arm mortality of 35%
at one year this corresponds to about 68 fewer deaths per 1000 patients
by one year. Versus ATG, the estimate also favoured PTCy, but was
imprecise (0·75 \[0·43–1·28\]). The survival estimate is supported by a
hazard-ratio sensitivity analysis: on the subset of studies reporting
(mostly adjusted) overall-survival hazard ratios, the pooled hazard
ratio was 0·88 \[0·66–1·14\] (k = 14), while the count-based odds ratio
on the same studies was 0·75 \[0·57–0·93\], thus indicating a a
consistent direction of effect (appendix S9). These findings extend the
BMT CTN 1703 RCT's matched-donor result[@bolanosmeade2023] across donor
types, conditioning regimens, and geographic settings, although the ATG
comparison was underpowered relative to C1.

The main contribution of this analysis is the clarification of
apparently contradictory infection findings. PTCy on days +3 and +4
eliminates alloreactive T cells (the intended GVHD-preventive
effect)[@kanakry2013; @wachsmuth2019] but depletes the nascent
pathogen-specific T-cell repertoire (a collateral cost)[@zhao2022]. For
the C1 comparisonm this revealed higher average risk of CMV reactivation
(1·20 \[0·87–1·65\]) and BSI (2·17 \[0·86–4·39\]), although both
intervals included the null.

A survival benefit for PTCy versus CNI prophylaxis is biologically
plausible as a consequence of GVHD suppression. GVHD and its treatment
are leading drivers of non-relapse mortality [@zeiser], and the
exploratory steroid-adjustment analysis (appendix S9) was compatible
with this GVHD–steroid pathway.

The C2 analysis provides a partial test of this framework. If CMV excess
were an intrinsic property of cyclophosphamide, it should persist
regardless of comparator. Instead, the CMV estimate versus ATG was
directionally opposite to the C1 estimate (C2 0·86 \[0·51–1·42\] versus
C1 1·20 \[0·87–1·65\]). A formal indirect comparison does not resolve
the difference: the posterior ratio of the two pooled odds ratios is
1·41 \[0·76–2·54\], and a comparator-class meta-regression pooling both
CMV datasets (k = 33) gave the same answer (0·71 \[0·41–1·20\]; appendix
S9). C1 and C2 also enroll different populations (predominantly
haploidentical versus matched-donor transplants), so comparator and
population effects cannot be separated. The depletion-depth ordering
(CNI-based \< PTCy \< ATG) is therefore a hypothesis compatible with the
data, but not proven. One external comparison is consistent with that
ordering: in a meta-analysis of combined ATG–PTCy prophylaxis in
haploidentical transplantation, CMV reactivation was more frequent with
the combination than with PTCy alone (risk ratio 1·42 \[1·03–1·95\]) but
did not differ from ATG alone (1·04 \[0·74–1·45\])[@luo2025].

BK virus does not fit this pattern: the elevation was nearly identical
against both comparators (C1 2·39 \[1·41–3·73\]; C2 2·49 \[1·08–6·24\];
ratio 0·96 \[0·33–2·50\]), compatible with a cyclophosphamide-specific
rather than class-wide depletion effect, and haemorrhagic cystitis is a
recognised cyclophosphamide effect[@kaphan2021; @ruggeri2015;
@chorao2025]. The C2 estimate rests on only three studies and remains
prior-influenced.

Several limitations warrant discussion. First, the evidence base is
predominantly observational and all pre-specified outcomes were rated
very low certainty under GRADE; selection bias, confounding by donor
type, and centre-level practice variation cannot be fully addressed by
meta-regression. Second, infection outcome definitions varied across
studies (for example, any CMV reactivation versus clinically significant
infection; any positive blood culture versus BSI requiring intensive
care), introducing measurement heterogeneity. Third, the IFI estimate
(0·63 \[0·19–2·44\]) rests on extreme between-study heterogeneity (τ =
1·28), is likely confounded by antifungal prophylaxis practices, and is
compatible with anything from a large reduction to a large increase.
Fourth, cohort deduplication removes the largest registry publications
from the seven affected outcomes where a smaller series reports the same
patients in more detail, so the survival and chronic GVHD totals rest on
fewer patients than the review's size suggests (appendix S12). Finally,
with two arms per study the random-effects model is just-identified, so
for sparse outcomes (k ≤ 6) the priors contribute materially to the
between-study standard deviation, and those credible intervals should be
read as lower bounds on the true uncertainty.

The within-PTCy comparison (C3) found no detectable differences between
regimen variants for any outcome. With k = 4–7 per outcome and wide
credible intervals, however, this is absence of evidence rather than
evidence of equivalence, and it should not be read as supporting
flexibility in dosing or backbone selection.

Depite these limitations, the analysis has potential clinical
implications. For centres already using PTCy, the infection costs are
best weighed in absolute terms: at the median comparator-arm rates, the
CMV odds ratio of 1·20 corresponds to about 46 additional reactivations
per 1000 patients by day +100 (a relative risk of about 1·09, not 1·20,
at a 48% baseline) and the BK odds ratio of 2·39 to about 134 additional
haemorrhagic cystitis cases per 1000 by day +100 from a 13% baseline,
while no elevation was detected for clinically significant CMV infection
(appendix S9). Whether these costs are shared with ATG-based regimens is
unresolved: the comparator-class test did not resolve the C1–C2
difference (appendix S9). Clinical strategies to mitigate these costs
should target T-cell reconstitution (adoptive T-cell therapies,
letermovir prophylaxis[@marty2017], earlier immunosuppression tapering)
rather than PTCy avoidance. The larger CMV estimate in studies published
from 2020 onward (odds ratio 1·43 \[0·97–2·06\]) is not explained by
letermovir-era prophylaxis: no arm in that cohort had letermovir use
recorded, and most of these cohorts enrolled before or across the
letermovir era (appendix S9), so the reasons for the trend remain
unclear. For NRM, optimising GVHD control remains a key strategy, as
approaches towards reducing GVHD severity and attendant steroid exposure
should translate into NRM benefit.

In conclusion, PTCy is associated with better overall survival and less
GVHD versus CNI-based prophylaxis, with less certain benefit versus ATG.
Infection estimates pattern differently by pathogen: CMV estimates are
directionally consistent with the depth of T-cell depletion without
establishing it, whereas BK virus elevation was similar across
comparators, compatible with a cyclophosphamide-specific mechanism. All
infection estimates were imprecise and these mechanistic readings are
hypothesis-generating. The potential excess infction risk of PTCy versus
CNIs may be best addressed through strategies targeting immune
reconstitution. The present analysis provides a unified framework for
interpreting the benefit–harm balance of PTCy; given very low certainty
of evidence for the pre-specified outcomes, its findings are hypotheses
for adequately powered randomised trials rather than a basis for
guideline recommendations.

## Contributors

REL, MS, and DPK developed the study protocol. REL and MS performed the
searches, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and statistical
analysis, and MS wrote the first draft of the report. MS and REL
verified the extracted data. DPK revised the manuscript. All authors had
full access to all the data in the study and had final responsibility
for the decision to submit for publication.

MS and REL declare no competing interests. DPK: honoraria and research

## Data sharing

Individual study-level data extracted for this systematic review,
including the complete extraction database and analytic datasets, are
available on a public GitHub repository
<https://github.com/lewis-id-lab/ptcy-infection.git>. The manuscript
source, including the notebooks that generate every table and figure, is
available with a rendered version for review at
<https://lewis-id-lab.github.io/ptcy-infection/>. The study protocol is
registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261372156).

## Use of artificial intelligence

AI-assisted extraction (Claude Code, Anthropic, Inc.) was used to aid
data extraction from original PDF source documents, and Posit Assistant
(Posit, Inc.) was used as an aid in R statistical code debugging within
the Positron integrated development environment. AI-extracted values
were manually verified against source publications. The authors take
full responsibility for the analysis and manuscript contents.

## Figures

![**Study selection (PRISMA 2020 flow diagram).** 4145 records were
identified from databases (EMBASE 2603, PubMed 1061, SCOPUS 481) and
1220 duplicates removed. 2925 records were screened and 2408 excluded at
title and abstract. 517 reports were sought for retrieval; 52 were not
retrieved or not in English (not recorded as separate counts). 465
full-text reports were assessed and 215 excluded ([appendix pp
6–14](appendix-preview.html#s2.-studies-excluded-at-full-text-screening-n214)).
250 studies were included in the systematic review; one publication
entered twice during extraction was removed during revision (appendix
S12). 105 unique studies contributed outcome data to the meta-analysis
(C1 72 studies; C2 27 studies; C3 13 studies; 7 studies contribute to
more than one comparison). Reference lists, citation tracking, and
PROSPERO registrations were also searched but yielded no separately
recorded reports, so the identification-via-other-methods branch of the
diagram shows zero.](figures/Figure1_PRISMA_flow_diagram){#fig-prisma}

{{< pagebreak >}}

![**Forest plot — overall survival, comparison 1 (PTCy vs CNI +
MTX/MMF).** Study rows are raw per-study odds ratios with Wald 95% CIs,
computed from the extracted event counts; the diamond is the pooled
Bayesian random-effects posterior median with 95% credible interval
(primary model M1). Events and totals of each arm and REML
inverse-variance weights are shown beside each study row; a 0·5
continuity correction was applied to zero cells when computing the Wald
intervals. k = 29 after cohort deduplication, removal of one duplicate
publication, and exclusion of cumulative-incidence-derived event counts
([appendix](appendix-preview.html#s12.-cohort-overlap)).](figures/Figure2_OS_forest_setB){#fig-os}

inverse-variance weights are shown beside each study row.
